source_text: Horum certe omnium contraria efficiunt, ne vir caput velet, scilicet quia non sit naturaliter consecutus ambitionem capillorum, quia radi sive tonderi non sit turpe illi, quia non propter illum. angeli exorbitarint, quia gloria et imago dei sit, quia caput eius Christus. Itaque cum de viro et muliere apostolus tractet cur illam oporteat velari, illum vero non, apparet cur et virginis silentium fecerit, eadem ratione scilicet virginem in muliere intellegendam sinens, qua et puerum ut in viro deputandum non nominavit, totum ordinem utriusque sexus propriis vocabulis complexus, mulieris et viri. Sic etiam Adam adhuc integer vir in Genesi est cognominatus: Vocabitur, inquit, mulier, quia de viro suo sumpta est. Sic vir Adam ante nuptiarum congressum, quemadmodum et Eva mulier. De utraque parte satis ad universam speciem cuiusque sexus apostolus pronuntiavit, et breviter et plene tam instructa definitione, Omnis, inquit, mulier. Quid est omnis, nisi omnis generis, omnis ordinis, omnis condicionis, omnis dignitatis, omnis aetatis? siquidem omne totum est et integrum et nulla sui parte defectum. Pars autem mulieris et virgo est. Aeque et de viro non velando, Omnis, inquit. Ecce duo diversa nomina, vir et mulier. Omnis uterque. Duae leges obnoxiae invicem, hinc velandi, inde nudandi. Igitur si eo, quod dictum sit omnis vir, commune est nomen viri etiam nondum viri, masculi investis, commune autem cum sit nomen secundum naturam, communis est et lex non velandi eius qui inter viros virgo est, secundum disciplinam, cur non praeiudicatum sit proinde et mulierem virginem omnem muliere nominata contineri consortio nominis, ut contineatur et communione legis? Si virgo mulier non est, nec vir investis est. Si non operitur virgo, quia mulier non sit, operiatur investis, quia vir non sit. Eiusdem virginitatis aequa sit venia. Sicut virgines non coguntur velari, ita pueri non iubeantur revelari. Cur ex parte definitionem apostoli agnoscimus absolutam circa omnem virum, nec retractamus quare non et puerum nominarit, ex parte autem praevaricamur, aeque absoluta ea circa omnem mulierem? Si quis, inquit, contentiosus est, nos talem consuetudinem non habemus, neque ecclesia dei. Ostendit contentionem aliquam de ista specie fuisse ad quam extinguendam toto compendio usus est, neque virginem nominans, ut ostenderet dubitandum de velanda non esse, et omnem nominans mulierem, cum nominasset virginem. Sic et ipsi Corinthii intellexerunt. Hodie denique virgines suas Corinthii velant. Quid docuerint apostoli qui didicerunt approbant.
thought_title: The apostle's silence about virgins means they are included in 'woman'
orientation: Tertullian is explaining why Paul's rule that men must not be veiled but women must be veiled applies equally to virgins, even though Paul did not name virgins explicitly.
pass_a_gloss: Certainly they produce the opposites of all these things, so that a man should not veil his head, namely because he has not naturally obtained the abundance of hair, because it is not shameful for him to be shaved or shorn, because the angels did not go astray on account of him, because he is the glory and image of God, because his head is Christ. And so, since the apostle treats about man and woman why she ought to be veiled, but he indeed not, it is clear why he also kept silence about the virgin, allowing of course the virgin to be understood in woman by the same reasoning by which he also did not name the boy, so that he should be counted in man, having embraced the whole order of each sex with the proper terms, of woman and of man. So also Adam, still untouched, is named man in Genesis: She will be called, it says, woman, because she was taken from her man. So Adam was man before the union of marriage, just as Eve also was woman. From each side the apostle pronounced sufficiently for the whole kind of each sex, both briefly and fully with so complete a definition: Every, he says, woman. What is every, unless of every kind, of every order, of every condition, of every rank, of every age? since every is whole and complete and lacking in no part of itself. But a part of woman is also the virgin. Equally also about the man not being veiled, Every, he says. Behold two different names, man and woman. Every of each. Two laws bound to each other, on this side of veiling, on that side of uncovering. Therefore if, because it was said every man, the name of man is common also to one not yet a man, to a beardless male, but since the name is common according to nature, the law of not veiling is also common to him who among men is a virgin according to discipline, why should it not have been prejudged likewise that every virgin woman, being named woman, is contained in the sharing of the name, so that she is contained also in the sharing of the law? If a virgin is not a woman, neither is a beardless youth a man. If a virgin is not covered, because she is not a woman, let a beardless youth be covered, because he is not a man. Let the pardon of the same virginity be equal. Just as virgins are not compelled to be veiled, so boys should not be ordered to be uncovered. Why do we recognize the apostle's definition as absolute concerning every man on one side, and do not question why he did not also name the boy, but on the other side we transgress, it being equally absolute concerning every woman? If anyone, he says, is contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the church of God. He shows that there had been some contention about this matter, for extinguishing which he used the whole summary, neither naming the virgin, so that he might show that there should be no doubt about her being veiled, and naming every woman, when he had named the virgin. So also the Corinthians themselves understood. Today finally the Corinthians veil their virgins. They approve what the apostles taught who learned it.

choices.why: The phrase refers to the natural fullness or luxuriance of hair given to women as a covering; 'abundance' captures the sense of natural endowment rather than a striving for it.
In context it means Adam before sexual union, still in his original virginal state; 'untouched' conveys the physical sense without importing modern moral overtones.
The term denotes a male not yet grown, lacking the beard that marks manhood; 'beardless youth' is the clearest English equivalent for the contrast with 'vir'.

choices.term: omnis generis, omnis ordinis, omnis condicionis, omnis dignitatis, omnis aetatis
choices.english: of every kind, of every order, of every condition, of every rank, of every age
choices.why: The rhetorical enumeration must be preserved in full to show the universality of 'every woman'; each term is rendered distinctly to avoid collapsing the categories.
rejected: of every sort, class, condition, rank, and age

choices.english: two laws bound to each other
choices.why: The laws of veiling and uncovering are mutually dependent and reciprocal; 'bound to each other' captures the reciprocal obligation Tertullian is arguing.
rejected: two laws subject to each other
two laws liable to each other

choices.why: Paul's brief statement 'every woman' is a comprehensive summary that settles the matter; 'whole summary' preserves the paradox of brevity and completeness.

pass_b_english: All these things, of course, produce the opposite for the man, so that he does not veil his head: because he has not naturally acquired a love of hair-display; because it is not shameful for him to be shaved or shorn; because the angels did not go astray on his account; because he is the glory and image of God; because Christ is his head (1 Corinthians 11:7, 3). So when the apostle discusses the man and the woman, why she ought to be veiled and he not, it is clear why he was also silent about the virgin: he allowed the virgin to be understood in the word 'woman' by the same reasoning by which he did not name the boy, since the boy is to be counted under 'man.' He embraced the whole order of each sex with its proper terms, 'woman' and 'man.' Thus Adam, still untouched, is called 'man' in Genesis: 'She shall be called woman,' he says, 'because she was taken from her man' (Genesis 2:23). So Adam was a man before the union of marriage, just as Eve was a woman. On both sides the apostle pronounced sufficiently for the whole class of each sex, and briefly and fully, with so complete a definition: 'Every woman,' he says (1 Corinthians 11:5). What is 'every' but of every kind, of every order, of every condition, of every rank, of every age? For 'every' is whole and complete and lacking no part of itself. And the virgin is a part of 'woman.' Likewise about the man not being veiled, he says 'Every' (1 Corinthians 11:4). See the two different names, man and woman. 'Every' applies to each. Two laws bound to each other: on one side veiling, on the other uncovering. Therefore, if because it says 'every man,' the name 'man' is common also to one not yet a man, a male not yet of age—and since the name is common according to nature, the law of not veiling is also common to him who is a virgin among men according to discipline—why should it not likewise be decided beforehand that every virgin woman is contained in the name 'woman' by the sharing of the name, so that she is contained also in the common law? If a virgin is not a woman, then a male not yet of age is not a man. If a virgin is not covered because she is not a woman, then let the male not yet of age be covered because he is not a man. Let the same virginity receive equal allowance. Just as virgins are not compelled to be veiled, so boys should not be ordered to be uncovered. Why do we recognize the apostle's definition as complete on one side, regarding every man, and do not question why he did not name the boy, yet on the other side we transgress, when it is equally complete regarding every woman? 'If anyone is contentious,' he says, 'we have no such custom, nor do the churches of God' (1 Corinthians 11:16). He shows that there had been some contention about this matter, to extinguish which he used the whole summary: not naming the virgin, to show that her being veiled is not to be doubted, and naming 'every woman' as though he had named the virgin. The Corinthians themselves understood it this way. In fact, to this day the Corinthians veil their virgins. What the apostles taught, those who learned from them confirm.

problems.quote: because he has not naturally received an abundance of hair
problems.source_quote: quia non sit naturaliter consecutus ambitionem capillorum
problems.why: 'Ambitio capillorum' means the desire for display/glory through hair, not 'abundance of hair.' The point is men don't naturally seek hair-display.
problems.fix: because he has not naturally acquired a love of hair-display
problems.ruling: Latin 'ambitio capillorum' = desire for hair glory; translation 'abundance of hair' changes meaning.

edits.old: because he has not naturally received an abundance of hair
edits.new: because he has not naturally acquired a love of hair-display

fixed: Changed 'abundance of hair' to 'love of hair-display' for 'ambitionem capillorum', which means desire for display through hair, not abundance.

problems.quote: not naming the virgin, to show that there should be no doubt about her being veiled
problems.source_quote: neque virginem nominans, ut ostenderet dubitandum de velanda non esse
problems.why: 'dubitandum ... non esse' means 'not to be doubted'; English 'no doubt about her being veiled' is ambiguous and could mean doubt exists.
problems.fix: not naming the virgin, to show that she is not to be doubted about being veiled
problems.ruling: Latin "neque virginem nominans, ut ostenderet dubitandum de velanda non esse" means doubt about veiling not being required, not certainty of veiling.

problems.why: Latin refers to the clothed man, not a beardless youth; English misidentifies the subject.
problems.fix: replace “beardless youth” with “the clothed man” (or “the man”) in both clauses.
problems.ruling: investis means 'unclothed/unveiled,' not 'beardless'; masculi investis is the male counterpart to virgin, not a beardless youth.

edits.old: not naming the virgin, to show that there should be no doubt about her being veiled
edits.new: not naming the virgin, to show that her being veiled is not to be doubted

edits.old: the beardless youth—and since the name is common according to nature, the law of not veiling is also common to him who is a virgin among men according to discipline—why should it not likewise be decided beforehand
edits.new: the clothed man—and since the name is common according to nature, the law of not veiling is also common to him who is a virgin among men according to discipline—why should it not likewise be decided beforehand

edits.old: then a beardless youth is not a man. If a virgin is not covered because she is not a woman, then let the beardless youth be covered because he is not a man.
edits.new: then a clothed man is not a man. If a virgin is not covered because she is not a woman, then let the clothed man be covered because he is not a man.

fixed: Fixed 'no doubt about her being veiled' to 'her being veiled is not to be doubted' to remove ambiguity; source 'dubitandum de velanda non esse' means it is not to be doubted.
Fixed 'beardless youth' to 'clothed man' in both clauses; source 'masculi investis' and 'investis' refer to the clothed man, not a beardless youth.

problems.why: investis means a male not yet of age (not yet in the toga), the opposite of clothed.
problems.fix: one not yet a man, a male not yet of age
problems.ruling: 'investis' means unclothed or beardless, i.e. a boy not yet grown. 'Clothed man' reverses it and contradicts 'nondum viri' in the same clause.

problems.quote: then a clothed man is not a man
problems.why: investis is the underage male, not a clothed man; the contrast with the virgin collapses.
problems.fix: then a male not yet of age is not a man
problems.ruling: 'nec vir investis est' parallels 'virgo mulier non est'. It means the immature male is not a man. 'Clothed' breaks the argument.

problems.quote: let the clothed man be covered
problems.why: The jussive is about the boy not yet of age, not a clothed man.
problems.fix: let the male not yet of age be covered because he is not a man
problems.ruling: 'operiatur investis, quia vir non sit' concerns the immature male, who is 'not a man'. 'Clothed man' is wrong and makes the sentence incoherent.

problems.quote: naming 'every woman' when he had named the virgin
problems.source_quote: omnem nominans mulierem, cum nominasset virginem
problems.why: cum with the pluperfect subjunctive means as if he had named her; he did not name the virgin.
problems.fix: naming 'every woman,' as though he had named the virgin
problems.ruling: The same sentence says 'neque virginem nominans'. Flat 'when he had named the virgin' contradicts it. The Latin means as though or since he had thereby named her.

fixed: 'the clothed man' misstates 'masculi investis' = a male not yet of age; fixed to 'a male not yet of age'.
'then a clothed man is not a man' misstates 'nec vir investis est'; fixed to 'then a male not yet of age is not a man'.

'when he had named the virgin' misstates 'cum nominasset virginem' = as though he had named her, since he did not name her; fixed to 'as though he had named the virgin'.
